title: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Shape
seo_title: Chemistry 11: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Shape Worksheets (BC Curriculum)
short_title: bonding, Lewis structures, VSEPR and polarity
standard_text: Bonding models: ionic, covalent and metallic bonding, Lewis structures, VSEPR shapes, electronegativity and polarity, and intermolecular forces. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Chemistry 11)
meta_desc: Free Chemistry 11 worksheets (BC Curriculum): bonding, Lewis structures, VSEPR and polarity. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Electron pairs push apart to give molecular shape.
key_sub: Polar bonds plus an uneven shape give a polar molecule.
body_html:
How to think about it

Ionic bonds form when electrons transfer from a metal to a non-metal; covalent bonds share electron pairs; metallic bonds have a sea of electrons. A Lewis structure shows the valence electrons around each atom.

VSEPR theory: electron pairs around a central atom repel, giving shapes such as linear (CO₂), trigonal planar (BF₃), tetrahedral (CH₄), trigonal pyramidal (NH₃) and bent (H₂O). A difference in electronegativity makes a bond polar; a polar molecule has an uneven charge, which affects intermolecular forces and boiling points.

Example

What is the shape of NH₃?

3 bonds + 1 lone pair

Answer: trigonal pyramidal

Example

Is CO₂ polar?

Polar bonds, but a linear shape

Answer: no, the dipoles cancel

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting lone pairs when choosing a shape.
  • Thinking every molecule with polar bonds is polar.
  • Mixing up intramolecular bonds and intermolecular forces.

faq.q: Why does water have a high boiling point?

items.q: What is the electronic configuration of the S<sup>2−</sup> ion?
items.e: The ion has 18 electrons, the same arrangement as a noble gas.

items.q: What is the electronic configuration of the O<sup>2−</sup> ion?
items.e: The ion has 10 electrons, the same arrangement as a noble gas.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between zinc (Zn) and nitrogen (N)?
items.e: A metal gives electrons to a non-metal.

items.q: What is the formula of barium phosphide?
items.e: Barium forms Ba<sup>2+</sup> and phosphorus forms P<sup>3−</sup>; the charges must add to zero.

items.q: How does a fluorine atom (proton number 9) form an ion?
items.e: Atoms gain or lose electrons to reach a noble gas electronic configuration.

items.q: Mg<sup>2+</sup> and N<sup>3−</sup> ions combine. What is the formula of the compound?
items.e: Use the lowest numbers that make the total charge zero: 3 × (+2) + 2 × (−3) = 0.

items.q: Na<sup>+</sup> and P<sup>3−</sup> ions combine. What is the formula of the compound?

items.q: What is the formula of strontium bromide?

items.q: Why does diamond have a very high melting point?
c: it has weak forces between molecules
each carbon is covalently bonded to four others in a giant network
items.e: All the strong covalent bonds must be broken.

items.q: What is graphene?
c: a single layer of carbon atoms in a hexagonal network
items.e: It is very strong and conducts electricity.

items.q: How can ethanol be separated from water?
c: fractional distillation, because their boiling points are different
items.e: Ethanol boils at 78 °C, water at 100 °C.

items.q: Why is an alloy usually harder than the pure metal?
c: atoms of different sizes disrupt the layers so they cannot slide easily
items.e: Bronze and steel are harder than copper and iron.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between sodium (Na) and zinc (Zn)?
items.e: Metal atoms share a sea of electrons.

items.q: How can pure water be obtained from sea water?
items.e: Water evaporates and condenses; salt is left behind.

items.q: Why do metals conduct electricity?
c: they have a sea of delocalized electrons that can move through the lattice
their ions move to the electrodes
items.e: Electrons carry the charge.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between sulfur (S) and fluorine (F)?
items.e: Two non-metals share electrons.

items.q: Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?
c: each carbon in graphite bonds to three others, leaving one delocalized electron
items.e: The electrons move along the layers.

items.q: Why are metals malleable?
c: the ions repel each other strongly
layers of cations can slide over each other while the delocalized electrons keep holding them together
items.e: Metallic bonding is not directional.

items.q: How can sand be separated from salt water?
items.e: Insoluble solids stay on the filter paper.

items.q: What is the shape of H<sub>2</sub>O?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs around the central atom: bent (non-linear).

items.q: What is the bond angle in PH<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: 3 bonding pairs, 1 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2.5°.

items.q: What is the bond angle in H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>?
items.e: 3 bonding pairs, 1 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2.5°.

items.q: How many σ and π bonds are there in ethyne, C₂H₂?
items.e: C≡C is one σ + two π; two C–H σ bonds.

items.q: What is the shape of H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>?
items.e: 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair around the central atom: pyramidal.

items.q: What is the shape of CCl<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: tetrahedral.

items.q: What is the shape of BeCl<sub>2</sub>?

items.q: What is the hybridization of carbon in CH₄?

items.q: What is a covalent bond?
c: a shared pair of electrons between two atoms
items.e: Each atom gets a stable configuration.

items.q: What is the shape of PCl₅?
items.e: PCl₅: trigonal bipyramidal.

items.q: What is the shape of PH<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair around the central atom: pyramidal.

items.q: What is the shape of ClF<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: 3 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs around the central atom: T-shaped.

items.q: What is the shape of XeF<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: 4 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs around the central atom: square planar.

items.q: What is the bond angle in BF<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: 3 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2.5°.

items.q: What is the bond angle in NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2.5°.

items.q: What is the shape of AlCl<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: 3 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: trigonal planar.

items.q: What is the bond angle in SF<sub>6</sub>?
items.e: 6 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2.5°.

items.q: How many covalent bonds does carbon (C) usually form?
items.e: It needs 4 more electrons for a full outer shell.

items.q: Oxygen (O) has 6 valence electrons. What is the formula of the simplest compound it forms with hydrogen?
items.e: It shares 2 electrons to fill its shell, so it bonds to 2 hydrogen atoms.

items.q: What is the shape of NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>?
items.e: 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: tetrahedral.

items.q: Which molecule does NOT obey the octet rule?
items.e: Boron has only six electrons in BF₃.

items.q: Electronegativity: calcium (Ca) = 1.00 and chlorine (Cl) = 3.16. What type of bond forms between them?
items.e: Difference = 2.16. Below 0.4: nonpolar; 0.4–1.7: polar covalent; above 1.7: ionic.

items.q: What is a sigma (σ) bond?
c: a bond formed by head-on overlap of orbitals
a bond formed by sideways overlap
items.e: It is stronger than a π bond.

items.q: What is the hybridization of carbon in CH₃COOH (the COOH carbon)?
items.e: CH₃COOH (the COOH carbon): sp².

items.q: What is the hybridization of carbon in HCN (the carbon)?
items.e: HCN (the carbon): sp.

items.q: Electronegativity: phosphorus (P) = 2.19 and bromine (Br) = 2.96. What type of bond forms between them?
items.e: Difference = 0.77. Below 0.4: nonpolar; 0.4–1.7: polar covalent; above 1.7: ionic.

items.q: How many electrons are shared in a double covalent bond?
items.e: Each bond is one shared pair (2 electrons).

items.q: Which molecule has a zero dipole moment even though its bonds are polar?
items.e: It is linear, so the bond dipoles cancel.

items.q: Fluorine (F) has 7 valence electrons. What is the formula of the simplest compound it forms with hydrogen?
items.e: It shares 1 electrons to fill its shell, so it bonds to 1 hydrogen atoms.

items.q: What is the shape of H₂O (oxygen)?
items.e: H₂O (oxygen): bent (V-shaped).

items.q: Chlorine (Cl) has 7 valence electrons. What is the formula of the simplest compound it forms with hydrogen?
items.e: It shares 1 electrons to fill its shell, so it bonds to 1 hydrogen atoms.

items.q: Electronegativity: fluorine (F) = 3.98 and iodine (I) = 2.66. What type of bond forms between them?
items.e: Difference = 1.32. Below 0.4: nonpolar; 0.4–1.7: polar covalent; above 1.7: ionic.

items.q: How many covalent bonds does nitrogen (N) usually form?

items.q: Electronegativity: oxygen (O) = 3.44 and boron (B) = 2.04. What type of bond forms between them?
items.e: Difference = 1.40. Below 0.4: nonpolar; 0.4–1.7: polar covalent; above 1.7: ionic.

items.q: Carbon (C) has 4 valence electrons. What is the formula of the simplest compound it forms with hydrogen?
items.e: It shares 4 electrons to fill its shell, so it bonds to 4 hydrogen atoms.

items.q: In a bond between iodine (I) and silicon (Si) (electronegativities 2.66 and 1.90), which atom gets a partial negative charge?
c: Neither; the electrons are shared equally.
items.e: The more electronegative atom pulls the shared electrons closer.

items.q: Electronegativity: fluorine (F) = 3.98 and carbon (C) = 2.55. What type of bond forms between them?
items.e: Difference = 1.43. Below 0.4: nonpolar; 0.4–1.7: polar covalent; above 1.7: ionic.

items.q: List from lowest to highest boiling point: helium (He), krypton (Kr), neon (Ne).
items.e: All have only intermolecular forces; more electrons (larger molar mass) means stronger forces.

items.q: List from lowest to highest boiling point: bromine (Br<sub>2</sub>), chlorine (Cl<sub>2</sub>), fluorine (F<sub>2</sub>).
items.e: All have only intermolecular forces; more electrons (larger molar mass) means stronger forces.

items.q: What is the strongest attraction between particles of magnesium oxide (MgO)?
c: ionic attractions (it is an ionic compound)
items.e: Ions attract each other strongly.

items.q: Which has the higher boiling point, chlorine (Cl<sub>2</sub>) or hexane (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>)?
c: They boil at the same temperature.
It depends only on the container.
items.e: Both have only intermolecular forces; hexane is larger (86 g/mol vs 71 g/mol), so its forces are stronger.
